Hey,

An existing Next.js CRM with ongoing bug fixes, small features, and API integration work sounds like a good fit for a part-time arrangement. The mix of UI/layout fixes, table views, filters, and form fields is the kind of work that benefits from someone who gets familiar with the codebase and stays on it, rather than a one-off task approach.

On the API integration fixes: my first step would be to trace the failing requests end to end, since these issues are often a mismatch between what the frontend component expects and what the endpoint actually returns. Checking the response shapes against the component's data display logic usually reveals the problem faster than patching symptoms in the UI layer.

For the UI bugs and layout issues, I would start by reproducing each one and checking whether it comes from CSS, conditional rendering, or stale data in the component state. That distinction matters because the fix and the testing approach differ for each case.

For the new features like filters and table views, I would want to see how the current data fetching is structured before writing anything, so the new components follow the patterns already in the app instead of introducing a second way of doing things.

A few questions to scope the start:. Is the CRM using the App Router or Pages Router in Next.js?. How is the backend built, and are the APIs documented or would I need to read the code to understand them?. What does the initial small set of tasks look like?

If you share the task list, I can give you a realistic estimate for the first batch and a timeline. I am available for the part-time hours you need and can start quickly.

Hey,

Your setup sounds like a common pattern: a Next.js storefront talking to a Node/Express backend, with bugs showing up at the seams between them. Those seams are usually where I'd start.

For the initial paid consultation, I'd map the data flow first: how the storefront fetches from your REST endpoints, where error handling is thin, and which API responses the UI assumes will always succeed. Most UI bugs in this kind of stack trace back to unhandled API states rather than the components themselves.

From there, I'd prioritize your list in this order: fix the storefront and admin UI bugs, then stabilize the API integrations, then build out filters, sorting, checkout fields, and order management on a solid foundation. Everything in type-safe TypeScript, so schema changes in MongoDB or Supabase don't silently break the frontend.

A few questions to scope this properly:. Is the admin panel part of the same Next.js app or a separate codebase?. Which database are you actually running today: SQL, MongoDB, or Supabase?. Are the REST integrations failing intermittently, or are there endpoints that have never worked correctly?

If the $ budget covers the initial consultation, I'd treat that as a working session: you get a concrete bug list and a prioritized fix plan, and we take it from there on an ongoing part-time basis.

When would be a good time for the codebase review?

Hey, a -day sprint to get an existing video collaboration platform production-ready usually comes down to a short list of blockers: unhandled auth edge cases, missing tenant isolation checks, background jobs that fail silently, and no test coverage around the critical paths. That is where I would start.

My first step would be a focused audit of the highest-risk areas: Google OAuth token refresh and scope handling, Gmail and Drive API error handling and rate limits, webhook verification, and multi-tenant data access controls. Those are the places where things work in demos and break in production.

From there I would fix the blockers in priority order, add targeted automated tests around auth, tenancy, and the job queue so regressions get caught, and hand you a short written list of anything that needs attention after the sprint with recommended fixes.

Relevant background: I recently worked on a SaaS platform with Google OAuth, Drive API integration, background jobs, and multi-tenant data separation, so I know the failure patterns specific to this stack.

One thing that would help me scope the two days accurately: is there a known incident or bug report that triggered this push to production readiness, or is this a general hardening pass before launch? If there is a specific failure, I want to make sure it gets fixed first.

If the scope sounds right, I can start immediately and work efficiently within the fixed budget.

Hey,

You need an MVP that proves the product works without overbuilding it, and the riskiest part is usually the LLM integration layer, not the dashboard. Getting token costs, latency, and fallback behavior right early saves a lot of rework later.

My approach for a first milestone:. Define the core user workflow end to end and cut everything that is not needed for a working demo.. Build the Python backend (FastAPI is a good lean choice) with the LLM API integration wrapped in a service layer, so you can swap providers without touching business logic.. Add a simple dashboard on top, plus auth and the basic subscription flow so it behaves like a real SaaS from day one.

For stack, I would keep it lean: FastAPI, Postgres, a lightweight frontend, and the LLM provider that best fits your use case and budget. I can also set up basic usage tracking so you know your per-user API cost before you launch.

A realistic timeline for an MVP at this scope is to weeks depending on how defined the workflows are. If you can share what the core user workflow looks like, I can give you a more precise estimate and flag anything that could be deferred to post-launch.

One question that would shape the architecture: do you expect users to bring their own LLM API keys, or should the platform handle all API usage under your account? That decision affects cost structure, rate limiting, and how I build the integration layer.

Happy to walk through the plan on a short call if useful.
